body.explanation: In the original FIFO, UDP offered 2 Gbps saturates l1, keeps the queue full, and tail-drops TCP, so all tested TCP types stay at or below 5792 bps. Replacing the sender FIFO with a scheduler gives each flow a service share, so Cubic reaches 476-482 Mbps while UDP takes the unused capacity. Queue length then matters only through TCP's class queue: q4 is below Cubic's ACK-clocked burst (inflight max 14 packets = 4 queue + 10 device queue) and drops 3416 TCP packets; q1000 permits a 952-packet backlog and 17.2 ms RTT; q100 caps the backlog at 100 packets (inflight max 110, RTT 2.1 ms) with only 71 drops, giving the highest measured goodput.

claims.text: In the original FIFO, UDP overload starves TCP: no tested TCP type exceeds 5792 bps.
A sender-side scheduler replacing the FIFO raises TCP goodput to hundreds of Mbps.
Under the scheduler, Cubic fills the scheduler share better than BBR, while UDP takes the unused capacity.
q100 is the best tested scheduler queue length: q4 loses to TCP drops, q1000 loses to backlog/RTT, and q100 is 1.16% above q1000.
The scheduler is work-conserving: TCP and UDP together use about the whole link, and TCP's rate is about its scheduler share.

The q4 drop count is compatible with only 1.2 s above 3.5 packets because drops occur in short full-queue bursts; q100's queue is usually above 3.5 but near the 100-packet cap only 1.5 s, giving 71 drops.
